correctness.rationale: Writing a cyclic quadruple by gap angles \(A,B,C,D\) with sum \(\pi\), the chord identity reduces the two relevant excesses to \(8R\cos((A-C)/2)\sin(B/2)\sin(D/2)\) and its symmetric counterpart. Thus the quadruple hyperbolicity is four times the minimum of the two corresponding products after the standard half-difference convention. For fixed opposite-gap total, concavity/balancing maximizes the sine product and minimizes the parity cosine penalty; the resulting upper envelope increases until the opposite totals are as equal as possible. Substitution gives exactly the four residue-class formulas and the listed balanced gaps. A fresh independent brute-force enumeration of every four-subset for \(4\le n\le30\) matched the closed formula to numerical precision; this finite replay supplements, rather than replaces, the analytic balancing proof.
correctness.risk: The metric is the ambient Euclidean chord metric on polygon vertices, not graph shortest-path distance or intrinsic circle arc distance.

value.rationale: Regular polygons are canonical finite samples of a Euclidean circle, and four-point hyperbolicity is a standard quantitative tree-likeness invariant. An exact all-\(n\) formula with maximizer geometry and the circle-limit constant is a natural closed classification, not an arbitrary numerical slice.
value.risk: The invariant is elementary enough that the result's value is concentrated in the exact sharp geometry and arithmetic oscillation.

final_claim: For the vertex set of a regular Euclidean \(n\)-gon of circumradius \(R\), equipped with ambient chord distance and the four-point convention in which the two largest opposite-pair sums differ by at most \(2\delta\), the exact Gromov hyperbolicity is the submitted modulo-four formula. Maximizers have the four cyclic gap counts as balanced as possible, and \(\delta_n\to(2-\sqrt2)R\), with equality for every \(4\mid n\).
limitations: Ambient Euclidean chord metric only; graph distance and arc-length metrics are different problems.
No claim is made for irregular polygons or arbitrary cyclic point sets.
